ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: You can usually choose your way out of forced obligations
ideas.statement: People generally have enough freedom over their jobs, customers, and location to trade money or conventional opportunity for less wasted time, if they decide to prioritize it.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Counting turns abstract time into felt scarcity
ideas.statement: Time itself is a smooth, continuous thing that's hard to judge as 'a lot' or 'a little.' But once you break it into small countable units — 52 weekends, 8 Christmases — the smallness becomes obvious in a way pure duration never makes clear.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: Self-chosen distractions are harder to escape than imposed ones
ideas.statement: Some time-wasting is forced on you by circumstance, but the kind you fall into voluntarily — arguing online, addictive pastimes — is worse, because it works by hijacking instincts you can't easily override, and getting better at hooking people is exactly what technology keeps doing.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: A result only counts if it could have come out otherwise
ideas.statement: An experiment or comparison only demonstrates something scientifically if it was genuinely capable of turning out differently, and if the same test can be repeated to check that it does turn out the same way again.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: A shrinking effect under better controls was never real
ideas.statement: If an experimental effect gets weaker and weaker as the methods used to detect it are tightened and its flaws are removed, that pattern itself shows the effect was an artifact rather than a real phenomenon that merely needed better proof.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: Cargo Cult Science copies form, not substance
ideas.statement: A field can reproduce every outward step and ritual of scientific work — controls, formulas, publications — and still fail to produce real results, because it is missing the one ingredient that actually makes the method work.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: Integrity means volunteering evidence against yourself
ideas.statement: Being honest as a scientist is not just refusing to state falsehoods; it means actively disclosing facts, alternative explanations, and doubts that could weaken your own claim, even when no one is asking for them.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: You must catch your own self-deception first
ideas.statement: The primary discipline in science is guarding against fooling yourself, since you are more easily deceived by your own hopes and expectations than any outside critic could deceive you; honesty toward others follows only after that.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: Synergy as a signature of genuine computation
ideas.statement: When a target neuron's activity depends on the joint pattern of its inputs in a way that cannot be recovered from any single input alone, that irreducible joint information is treated as evidence the target is combining and transforming its inputs into something new, not just relaying them.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Densely interconnected hub neurons are the network's computational core
ideas.statement: Because rich-club neurons are unusually densely interconnected and carry a disproportionate share of information flow, they are treated as the sites where the circuit does its heaviest computational work, not merely as busy relay points.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: An inferred statistical network stands in for real circuit wiring
ideas.statement: A set of statistically significant directed dependencies (transfer-entropy edges) between recorded units is treated as tracing the actual pathways along which information travels in the underlying biological circuit, rather than as a purely correlational summary of the recordings.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: Undirected correlation versus directed flow as different questions
ideas.statement: A measure of shared statistical dependence between two variables answers a different question than a measure of how one variable's past uniquely shapes another's future beyond what the second variable's own history already explains; the first is functional similarity, the second is directed influence.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: Joint information need not equal the sum of individual contributions
ideas.statement: The total information that a group of sources jointly carries about a target can be greater or less than the sum of what each source carries on its own, revealing hidden synergy or redundancy that is invisible if sources are examined one at a time.

ideas.label: I6
ideas.name: Redundancy has no unique definition within classical information theory
ideas.statement: The equations relating total joint information to redundant, unique, and synergistic pieces are underdetermined; ordinary Shannon theory supplies the joint and marginal mutual informations but leaves the split among redundancy, uniqueness, and synergy unfixed, so an extra measure or assumption must be introduced to pin it down.

ideas.label: I7
ideas.name: The number of decomposition components explodes combinatorially with source count
ideas.statement: The number of distinct redundant, unique, and synergistic pieces produced when decomposing information from k sources grows according to the Dedekind numbers, a sequence that increases so fast that a complete decomposition becomes computationally and practically unmanageable once there are more than a handful of sources.

ideas.label: I8
ideas.name: A partial order over source-combinations plus Möbius inversion yields a unique decomposition
ideas.statement: Once a redundancy function is fixed, all possible non-redundant combinations of sources can be arranged in a lattice ordered by which combinations subsume which others, and applying Möbius inversion over that lattice assigns a single well-defined value to every distinct mode of information sharing, exhaustively accounting for the total.

ideas.label: I9
ideas.name: Synergy peaks at intermediate, not maximal, input similarity
ideas.statement: As two input sources feeding a common target become more statistically similar to each other, the synergistic information they jointly provide about the target first rises with that similarity but then falls once the sources become too redundant, so the greatest joint computation happens at an intermediate rather than a maximal level of input correlation.

ideas.label: I10
ideas.name: Information measures can be defined event-by-event, not just as averages
ideas.statement: Rather than reporting only the expected (dataset-averaged) amount of shared information, an information quantity can instead be computed separately for every individual observed configuration of the variables, producing a value that changes at every moment in time rather than one summary number.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: Physical after-effects as stand-ins for direct measurement
ideas.statement: When a transient event cannot be measured directly, the marks, residues, or timed sounds it leaves behind can be treated as reliable stand-ins for measuring its physical properties, such as speed, energy, or composition.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Professional training upgrades eyewitness reliability
ideas.statement: A person's scientific or professional training is presented as making their account of a strange, brief event more trustworthy and more scientifically usable than an ordinary bystander's account.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: Popular imagery can outlive and distort the documented facts
ideas.statement: A dramatic story or picture about a phenomenon can take hold in public imagination and persist as its defining image even after the factual record shows something more mundane.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: Ball lightning may be several different phenomena
ideas.statement: The seemingly contradictory reports of ball lightning may not describe one single physical process but several distinct types or mechanisms lumped under one name.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: Isolated, uncoordinated research fragments a field
ideas.statement: When data collection, theorizing, and laboratory testing on a phenomenon proceed separately without coordination, the result is a scattered, inconclusive body of research rather than a converging science.

ideas.label: I6
ideas.name: Independent lightning-detection data can corroborate testimony
ideas.statement: Matching an eyewitness account's time and place against automated lightning-location network records provides an independent check on an otherwise unverifiable personal report.

ideas.label: I7
ideas.name: Elite samples reveal reporting biases when compared to mass data
ideas.statement: Comparing a small set of expert-observer reports against a much larger general public database can expose how the type of observer shapes which characteristics of an event get noticed and recorded.

ideas.label: I8
ideas.name: Shock trauma splits into separate immediate and lasting effects
ideas.statement: A sudden physical shock can produce two distinct kinds of harm that must be diagnosed separately: a short-lived direct physiological disruption and a separate, longer-lasting psychological disorder.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: Long shots are worth it when the payoff is huge
ideas.statement: An attempt's worth is its chance of success times the size of the payoff. A small chance at an enormous gain can beat a sure modest one, and when single outcomes can't be predicted, making many attempts is the way to collect the rare big win.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Greedy choices can strand you on a local peak
ideas.statement: A greedy method always takes whichever next step looks best right now. Such a method can get stuck on a local maximum: a spot better than everything nearby but worse than the best spot overall, which could only be reached by first passing through something that looks worse.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: A successful discovery stops surprising later readers
ideas.statement: Because an essay works by teaching, its value depends on what readers do not yet know. When its ideas win and become common knowledge, the essay keeps its importance but loses its surprise. So lasting, evergreen appeal requires ideas that never fully sink in.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: Questions need inspiration; answers yield to persistence
ideas.statement: Answers can be ground out by rewriting until they are right, so effort covers them. Good questions come from inspiration, often from curiosity about some odd small puzzle, and in the best work this supply of questions is what limits quality.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: Writing turns vague ideas into fixable wrong ones
ideas.statement: Committing to specific words makes a hazy thought concrete enough to see where it is broken. Strict rereading then exposes gaps between the draft and the truth, and those gaps often point to new ideas or hidden false assumptions.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: Skull form reliably reveals inner character
ideas.statement: The shape and proportion of a person's head can be read to accurately disclose the strength of their underlying mental faculties, without need for further behavioral evidence.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Harmony of faculties, not raw strength, is what matters
ideas.statement: Success and virtue come from the faculties working together in balance; a powerful faculty left uncoordinated with the rest produces failure or vice rather than advantage.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: Marital happiness depends on matching combinations of faculties
ideas.statement: Compatibility between partners is a matter of which faculties and temperaments each possesses, and a marriage fails or succeeds according to whether these combinations suit each other, independent of wealth or appearance.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: Innate organization fixes the ceiling of what a person can become
ideas.statement: A person can improve and even excel within their natural sphere, but effort and desire cannot carry them past the limits set by their inborn mental and physical organization.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: Reading a child's organization early allows pre-emptive correction
ideas.statement: Because a child's dominant faculties can be identified before they fully manifest in behavior, a parent or teacher can intervene in advance to prevent an excessive faculty from ever becoming a problem, rather than reacting after the fact.

ideas.label: I6
ideas.name: Mental states can cause and cure bodily illness
ideas.statement: The mind acts on the body directly, so that disappointment, grief, or a strong will can produce genuine physical prostration or resist medical treatment, and a change of mental state can restore health.

ideas.label: I7
ideas.name: The same faculty is virtue or vice depending on degree and control
ideas.statement: No mental faculty is bad in itself; the identical trait that drives success when exercised proportionately becomes crime or disease when it is excessive, deficient, or unchecked by the moral faculties.

ideas.label: I8
ideas.name: Guilt should be measured against a person's given moral equipment
ideas.statement: Two people who commit the same act are not equally guilty; the one whose organization gave them more capacity for restraint and better moral faculties bears greater responsibility than one whose organization left them poorly equipped to resist.

stops.quote: Having kids showed me how to convert a continuous quantity, time, into discrete quantities. You only get 52 weekends with your 2 year old. If Christmas-as-magic lasts from say ages 3 to 10, you only get to watch your child experience it 8 t
stops.quoteFull: Having kids showed me how to convert a continuous quantity, time, into discrete quantities. You only get 52 weekends with your 2 year old. If Christmas-as-magic lasts from say ages 3 to 10, you only get to watch your child experience it 8 times.
stops.paragraph: Having kids showed me how to convert a continuous quantity, time, into discrete quantities. You only get 52 weekends with your 2 year old. If Christmas-as-magic lasts from say ages 3 to 10, you only get to watch your child experience it 8 times. And while it's impossible to say what is a lot or a little of a continuous quantity like time, 8 is not a lot of something. If you had a handful of 8 peanuts, or a shelf of 8 books to choose from, the quantity would definitely seem limited, no matter what your lifespan was.
stops.cue: Notice how counting small numbers changes how 'short' time feels.

stops.quote: Relentlessly prune bullshit, don't wait to do things that matter, and savor the time you have. That's what you do when life is short.
stops.quoteFull: Relentlessly prune bullshit, don't wait to do things that matter, and savor the time you have. That's what you do when life is short.
stops.paragraph: Relentlessly prune bullshit, don't wait to do things that matter, and savor the time you have. That's what you do when life is short.
stops.cue: Look for the three-part summary of what to do with limited time.

stops.quote: If you find yourself thinking that life is too short for something, you should try to eliminate it if you can.
stops.quoteFull: If you find yourself thinking that life is too short for something, you should try to eliminate it if you can.
stops.paragraph: It has for me. It means arguments of the form "Life is too short for x" have great force. It's not just a figure of speech to say that life is too short for something. It's not just a synonym for annoying. If you find yourself thinking that life is too short for something, you should try to eliminate it if you can.
stops.cue: Ask what test the author proposes for deciding what to cut from life.

stops.quote: There are two ways this kind of thing gets into your life: it's either forced on you, or it tricks you.
stops.quoteFull: There are two ways this kind of thing gets into your life: it's either forced on you, or it tricks you.
stops.paragraph: There are two ways this kind of thing gets into your life: it's either forced on you, or it tricks you. To some extent you have to put up with the bullshit forced on you by circumstances. You need to make money, and making money consists mostly of errands. Indeed, the law of supply and demand ensures that: the more rewarding some kind of work is, the cheaper people will do it. It may be that less bullshit is forced on you than you think, though. There has always been a stream of people who opt out of the default grind and go live somewhere where opportunities are fewer in the conventional sense, but life feels more authentic. This could become more common.
stops.cue: Look for the two ways unwanted obligations enter your life.

stops.quote: Perhaps a better solution is to look at the problem from the other end. Cultivate a habit of impatience about the things you most want to do. Don't wait before climbing that mountain or writing that book or visiting your mother. You don't n
stops.quoteFull: Perhaps a better solution is to look at the problem from the other end. Cultivate a habit of impatience about the things you most want to do. Don't wait before climbing that mountain or writing that book or visiting your mother. You don't need to be constantly reminding yourself why you shouldn't wait. Just don't wait.
stops.paragraph: The usual way to avoid being taken by surprise by something is to be consciously aware of it. Back when life was more precarious, people used to be aware of death to a degree that would now seem a bit morbid. I'm not sure why, but it doesn't seem the right answer to be constantly reminding oneself of the grim reaper hovering at everyone's shoulder. Perhaps a better solution is to look at the problem from the other end. Cultivate a habit of impatience about the things you most want to do. Don't wait before climbing that mountain or writing that book or visiting your mother. You don't need to be constantly reminding yourself why you shouldn't wait. Just don't wait.
stops.cue: Notice what habit the author recommends instead of reminding yourself not to wait.

stops.quote: When someone contradicts you, they're in a sense attacking you. Sometimes pretty overtly. Your instinct when attacked is to defend yourself. But like a lot of instincts, this one wasn't designed for the world we now live in. Counterintuitiv
stops.quoteFull: When someone contradicts you, they're in a sense attacking you. Sometimes pretty overtly. Your instinct when attacked is to defend yourself. But like a lot of instincts, this one wasn't designed for the world we now live in. Counterintuitive as it feels, it's better most of the time not to defend yourself. Otherwise these people are literally taking your life.
stops.paragraph: But while some amount of bullshit is inevitably forced on you, the bullshit that sneaks into your life by tricking you is no one's fault but your own. And yet the bullshit you choose may be harder to eliminate than the bullshit that's forced on you. Things that lure you into wasting your time have to be really good at tricking you. An example that will be familiar to a lot of people is arguing online. When someone contradicts you, they're in a sense attacking you. Sometimes pretty overtly. Your instinct when attacked is to defend yourself. But like a lot of instincts, this one wasn't designed for the world we now live in. Counterintuitive as it feels, it's better most of the time not to defend yourself. Otherwise these people are literally taking your life.
stops.cue: Look for what instinct makes self-chosen distractions hard to resist.

stops.quote: One heuristic for distinguishing stuff that matters is to ask yourself whether you'll care about it in the future. Fake stuff that matters usually has a sharp peak of seeming to matter. That's how it tricks you. The area under the curve is
stops.quoteFull: One heuristic for distinguishing stuff that matters is to ask yourself whether you'll care about it in the future. Fake stuff that matters usually has a sharp peak of seeming to matter. That's how it tricks you. The area under the curve is small, but its shape jabs into your consciousness like a pin.
stops.paragraph: One heuristic for distinguishing stuff that matters is to ask yourself whether you'll care about it in the future. Fake stuff that matters usually has a sharp peak of seeming to matter. That's how it tricks you. The area under the curve is small, but its shape jabs into your consciousness like a pin.
stops.cue: Look for the test suggested for telling real value from fake urgency.

stops.quote: If life is short, we should expect its shortness to take us by surprise. And that is just what tends to happen. You take things for granted, and then they're gone.
stops.quoteFull: If life is short, we should expect its shortness to take us by surprise. And that is just what tends to happen. You take things for granted, and then they're gone.
stops.paragraph: If life is short, we should expect its shortness to take us by surprise. And that is just what tends to happen. You take things for granted, and then they're gone. You think you can always write that book, or climb that mountain, or whatever, and then you realize the window has closed. The saddest windows close when other people die. Their lives are short too. After my mother died, I wished I'd spent more time with her. I lived as if she'd always be there. And in her typical quiet way she encouraged that illusion. But an illusion it was. I think a lot of people make the same mistake I did.
stops.cue: Notice how the author says life's shortness tends to catch us off guard.

stops.quote: So I call these things Cargo Cult Science, because they follow all the apparent precepts and forms of scientific investigation, but they’re missing something essential, because the planes don’t land.
stops.quoteFull: So I call these things Cargo Cult Science, because they follow all the apparent precepts and forms of scientific investigation, but they’re missing something essential, because the planes don’t land.
stops.paragraph: I think the educational and psychological studies I mentioned are examples of what I would like to call Cargo Cult Science. In the South Seas there is a Cargo Cult of people. During the war they saw airplanes land with lots of good materials, and they want the same thing to happen now. So they’ve arranged to make things like runways, to put fires along the sides of the runways, to make a wooden hut for a man to sit in, with two wooden pieces on his head like headphones and bars of bamboo sticking out like antennas—he’s the controller—and they wait for the airplanes to land. They’re doing everything right. The form is perfect. It looks exactly the way it looked before. But it doesn’t work. No airplanes land. So I call these things Cargo Cult Science, because they follow all the apparent precepts and forms of scientific investigation, but they’re missing something essential, because the planes don’t land.
stops.cue: Look for what the cargo cult imitates but still lacks.

stops.quote: If you make a theory, for example, and advertise it, or put it out, then you must also put down all the facts that disagree with it, as well as those that agree with it.
stops.quoteFull: If you make a theory, for example, and advertise it, or put it out, then you must also put down all the facts that disagree with it, as well as those that agree with it.
stops.paragraph: Details that could throw doubt on your interpretation must be given, if you know them. You must do the best you can—if you know anything at all wrong, or possibly wrong—to explain it. If you make a theory, for example, and advertise it, or put it out, then you must also put down all the facts that disagree with it, as well as those that agree with it. There is also a more subtle problem. When you have put a lot of ideas together to make an elaborate theory, you want to make sure, when explaining what it fits, that those things it fits are not just the things that gave you the idea for the theory; but that the finished theory makes something else come out right, in addition.
stops.cue: What extra step does honest theorizing require beyond stating your claim?

stops.quote: The first principle is that you must not fool yourself—and you are the easiest person to fool. So you have to be very careful about that. After you’ve not fooled yourself, it’s easy not to fool other scientists. You just have to be honest i
stops.quoteFull: The first principle is that you must not fool yourself—and you are the easiest person to fool. So you have to be very careful about that. After you’ve not fooled yourself, it’s easy not to fool other scientists. You just have to be honest in a conventional way after that.
stops.paragraph: The first principle is that you must not fool yourself—and you are the easiest person to fool. So you have to be very careful about that. After you’ve not fooled yourself, it’s easy not to fool other scientists. You just have to be honest in a conventional way after that.
stops.cue: Who does Feynman say is hardest to avoid deceiving, and why?

stops.quote: Why didn’t they discover that the new number was higher right away? It’s a thing that scientists are ashamed of—this history—because it’s apparent that people did things like this: When they got a number that was too high above Millikan’s,
stops.quoteFull: Why didn’t they discover that the new number was higher right away? It’s a thing that scientists are ashamed of—this history—because it’s apparent that people did things like this: When they got a number that was too high above Millikan’s, they thought something must be wrong—and they would look for and find a reason why something might be wrong. When they got a number closer to Millikan’s value they didn’t look so hard. And so they eliminated the numbers that were too far off, and did other things like that.
stops.paragraph: Why didn’t they discover that the new number was higher right away? It’s a thing that scientists are ashamed of—this history—because it’s apparent that people did things like this: When they got a number that was too high above Millikan’s, they thought something must be wrong—and they would look for and find a reason why something might be wrong. When they got a number closer to Millikan’s value they didn’t look so hard. And so they eliminated the numbers that were too far off, and did other things like that. We’ve learned those tricks nowadays, and now we don’t have that kind of a disease.
stops.cue: Notice how the scientists treated numbers that differed from the expected value.

stops.quote: In other words, publication probability depends upon the answer. That should not be done.
stops.quoteFull: In other words, publication probability depends upon the answer. That should not be done.
stops.paragraph: One example of the principle is this: If you’ve made up your mind to test a theory, or you want to explain some idea, you should always decide to publish it whichever way it comes out. If we only publish results of a certain kind, we can make the argument look good. We must publish both kinds of result. For example—let’s take advertising again—suppose some particular cigarette has some particular property, like low nicotine. It’s published widely by the company that this means it is good for you—they don’t say, for instance, that the tars are a different proportion, or that something else is the matter with the cigarette. In other words, publication probability depends upon the answer. That should not be done.
stops.cue: Ask what should never influence whether a result gets published.

stops.quote: If your answer happens to come out in the direction the government or the politicians like, they can use it as an argument in their favor; if it comes out the other way, they don’t publish it at all. That’s not giving scientific advice.
stops.quoteFull: If your answer happens to come out in the direction the government or the politicians like, they can use it as an argument in their favor; if it comes out the other way, they don’t publish it at all. That’s not giving scientific advice.
stops.paragraph: I say that’s also important in giving certain types of government advice. Supposing a senator asked you for advice about whether drilling a hole should be done in his state; and you decide it would he better in some other state. If you don’t publish such a result, it seems to me you’re not giving scientific advice. You’re being used. If your answer happens to come out in the direction the government or the politicians like, they can use it as an argument in their favor; if it comes out the other way, they don’t publish it at all. That’s not giving scientific advice.
stops.cue: Watch how political convenience can distort what counts as advice.

stops.paragraph: Now, from a scientific standpoint, that is an A‑Number‑l experiment. That is the experiment that makes rat‑running experiments sensible, because it uncovers the clues that the rat is really using—not what you think it’s using. And that is the experiment that tells exactly what conditions you have to use in order to be careful and control everything in an experiment with rat‑running.
stops.cue: What made this rat experiment count as rigorous, according to Feynman?

stops.quote: They just went right on running rats in the same old way, and paid no attention to the great discoveries of Mr. Young, and his papers are not referred to, because he didn’t discover anything about the rats. In fact, he discovered all the th
stops.quoteFull: They just went right on running rats in the same old way, and paid no attention to the great discoveries of Mr. Young, and his papers are not referred to, because he didn’t discover anything about the rats. In fact, he discovered all the things you have to do to discover something about rats. But not paying attention to experiments like that is a characteristic of Cargo Cult Science.
stops.paragraph: I looked into the subsequent history of this research. The subsequent experiment, and the one after that, never referred to Mr. Young. They never used any of his criteria of putting the corridor on sand, or being very careful. They just went right on running rats in the same old way, and paid no attention to the great discoveries of Mr. Young, and his papers are not referred to, because he didn’t discover anything about the rats. In fact, he discovered all the things you have to do to discover something about rats. But not paying attention to experiments like that is a characteristic of Cargo Cult Science.
stops.cue: Why did later researchers ignore this careful experiment's lesson?

stops.quote: All the parapsychologists are looking for some experiment that can be repeated—that you can do again and get the same effect—statistically, even. They run a million rats—no, it’s people this time—they do a lot of things and get a certain st
stops.quoteFull: All the parapsychologists are looking for some experiment that can be repeated—that you can do again and get the same effect—statistically, even. They run a million rats—no, it’s people this time—they do a lot of things and get a certain statistical effect. Next time they try it they don’t get it any more. And now you find a man saying that it is an irrelevant demand to expect a repeatable experiment. This is science?
stops.paragraph: Another example is the ESP experiments of Mr. Rhine, and other people. As various people have made criticisms—and they themselves have made criticisms of their own experiments—they improve the techniques so that the effects are smaller, and smaller, and smaller until they gradually disappear. All the parapsychologists are looking for some experiment that can be repeated—that you can do again and get the same effect—statistically, even. They run a million rats—no, it’s people this time—they do a lot of things and get a certain statistical effect. Next time they try it they don’t get it any more. And now you find a man saying that it is an irrelevant demand to expect a repeatable experiment. This is science?
stops.cue: What test should any claimed effect be able to pass, and why does it fail here?

stops.quote: It is very dangerous to have such a policy in teaching—to teach students only how to get certain results, rather than how to do an experiment with scientific integrity.
stops.quoteFull: It is very dangerous to have such a policy in teaching—to teach students only how to get certain results, rather than how to do an experiment with scientific integrity.
stops.paragraph: This man also speaks about a new institution, in a talk in which he was resigning as Director of the Institute of Parapsychology. And, in telling people what to do next, he says that one of the things they have to do is be sure they only train students who have shown their ability to get PSI results to an acceptable extent—not to waste their time on those ambitious and interested students who get only chance results. It is very dangerous to have such a policy in teaching—to teach students only how to get certain results, rather than how to do an experiment with scientific integrity.
stops.cue: Think about what students learn when only taught to get a desired result.

stops.quote: So I wish to you—I have no more time, so I have just one wish for you—the good luck to be somewhere where you are free to maintain the kind of integrity I have described, and where you do not feel forced by a need to maintain your position
stops.quoteFull: So I wish to you—I have no more time, so I have just one wish for you—the good luck to be somewhere where you are free to maintain the kind of integrity I have described, and where you do not feel forced by a need to maintain your position in the organization, or financial support, or so on, to lose your integrity.
stops.paragraph: So I wish to you—I have no more time, so I have just one wish for you—the good luck to be somewhere where you are free to maintain the kind of integrity I have described, and where you do not feel forced by a need to maintain your position in the organization, or financial support, or so on, to lose your integrity. May you have that freedom. May I also give you one last bit of advice: Never say that you’ll give a talk unless you know clearly what you’re going to talk about and more or less what you’re going to say.
stops.cue: What condition does Feynman wish for his listeners to keep their integrity?

stops.quote: It is known, however, that such processes are distributed over integrative interactions in neural circuits throughout the brain and involve large numbers of interacting neurons. We refer to this collective activity as neural information pro
stops.quoteFull: It is known, however, that such processes are distributed over integrative interactions in neural circuits throughout the brain and involve large numbers of interacting neurons. We refer to this collective activity as neural information processing.
stops.paragraph: A grand challenge of modern neuroscience is to discover how brains “process information”. Though there is debate regarding what information processing means precisely, it is clear that brains take in sensory signals from the environment and use that information to generate adaptive behavior informed by their surroundings. The ways that sensory information is modified and transformed are poorly understood. It is known, however, that such processes are distributed over integrative interactions in neural circuits throughout the brain and involve large numbers of interacting neurons. We refer to this collective activity as neural information processing.
stops.cue: Notice how the authors describe neural computation as distributed across many interacting neurons.

stops.quote: Historically, there have been two key limitations hindering the study of information processing by neural circuits. The first was a lack of appropriate data, since the analysis of synergistic dynamics requires large amounts of data to accur
stops.quoteFull: Historically, there have been two key limitations hindering the study of information processing by neural circuits. The first was a lack of appropriate data, since the analysis of synergistic dynamics requires large amounts of data to accurately infer the structure of multivariate dependence.
stops.paragraph: Historically, there have been two key limitations hindering the study of information processing by neural circuits. The first was a lack of appropriate data, since the analysis of synergistic dynamics requires large amounts of data to accurately infer the structure of multivariate dependence. Until recently, such data were difficult to access. In the last decade, however, with innovative new electrical and optical recording technologies that can record from hundreds or thousands of neurons at sub-millisecond temporal resolution, this limitation has abated considerably. The second was a lack of appropriate analytical approaches. Despite the recent explosion of data, a rendering processes is still needed to extract interpretable insights from terabytes of recordings.
stops.cue: What two obstacles does the piece say historically blocked studying information processing in circuits?

stops.quote: I(X;Y) measures how our ability to correctly infer the state of X changes, depending on whether we are accounting for (potentially) shared dependencies with Y. It can be thought of as a nonlinear correlation between two patterns of activity
stops.quoteFull: I(X;Y) measures how our ability to correctly infer the state of X changes, depending on whether we are accounting for (potentially) shared dependencies with Y. It can be thought of as a nonlinear correlation between two patterns of activity [3,13].
stops.paragraph: Mutual information [12] can measure the dependence in the spiking between two neurons: I(X;Y) := ∑ x∈X y∈Y P(x, y)log2 P(x|y) P(x) (1) where P(x, y) is the probability distribution of the joint state of X and Y, P(x) is the marginal probability of X, and P(x|y) is the conditional probability X = x given that Y = y. I(X;Y) measures how our ability to correctly infer the state of X changes, depending on whether we are accounting for (potentially) shared dependencies with Y. It can be thought of as a nonlinear correlation between two patterns of activity [3,13]. This similarity is related to functional connectivity [14]. It does not, however, quantify information transfer between the neurons, as it is an undirected measure that describes the instantaneous dependency between two variables and has no notion of the time-directed structure that we intuitively understand as “transfer” or “flow.”
stops.cue: Ask what kind of relationship between two activity patterns mutual information is capturing.

stops.quote: TE is understood as quantifying how much the past of the source variable reduces our uncertainty about the future of the target variable, after accounting for information disclosed by the target variable’s own past (autocorrelation). Wherea
stops.quoteFull: TE is understood as quantifying how much the past of the source variable reduces our uncertainty about the future of the target variable, after accounting for information disclosed by the target variable’s own past (autocorrelation). Whereas mutual information is a measure of functional connectivity, transfer entropy measures effective connectivity [14]. In other words, transfer entropy provides a measure of information propagation.
stops.paragraph: Transfer entropy [11] is well suited to measuring how much the past activity of one neuron (e.g., Xp) accounts for the immediate future activity of another neuron (e.g., Yt+1), conditioned on Y’s own past (Yp): TE(X → Y) := (2) ∑ yt+1∈Y xp∈Xp yp∈Yp P(yt+1, yp, xp)log2 P(yt+1|xp, yp) P(yt+1|yp) TE(X → Y) is read as the transfer entropy from X’s past to Y’s future. It is important to note that Xp does not necessarily have to be a single moment or bin but can be a multi-dimensional and potentially non-uniform embedding [15–17]. TE is understood as quantifying how much the past of the source variable reduces our uncertainty about the future of the target variable, after accounting for information disclosed by the target variable’s own past (autocorrelation). Whereas mutual information is a measure of functional connectivity, transfer entropy measures effective connectivity [14]. In other words, transfer entropy provides a measure of information propagation. In addition to measuring the magnitude of information flow between two neurons, in the special case of binary signals the TE can be modified to also provide a measure of excitation/inhibition balance using the sorted local transfer entropy [18].
stops.cue: Compare what transfer entropy measures against plain mutual information - what extra question does it answer?

stops.quote: Information transfer captures the overall “flow” of information through the system; however, it is limited in its ability to reveal how different streams of information “interact” and how neurons produce novel or modified information from m
stops.quoteFull: Information transfer captures the overall “flow” of information through the system; however, it is limited in its ability to reveal how different streams of information “interact” and how neurons produce novel or modified information from multiple sources [19]. How does one examine information processing itself? We propose that one successful avenue is that of multivariate information decomposition [1].
stops.paragraph: Information transfer captures the overall “flow” of information through the system; however, it is limited in its ability to reveal how different streams of information “interact” and how neurons produce novel or modified information from multiple sources [19]. How does one examine information processing itself? We propose that one successful avenue is that of multivariate information decomposition [1].
stops.cue: Look for what information-transfer measures cannot tell us about how neurons combine their inputs.

stops.quote: If the left-hand side of Equation (4) (the “whole”) is greater than the right-hand side (the sum of the “parts”), then there is some information about Y that is disclosed by the joint state of all the neurons that is not disclosed by any in
stops.quoteFull: If the left-hand side of Equation (4) (the “whole”) is greater than the right-hand side (the sum of the “parts”), then there is some information about Y that is disclosed by the joint state of all the neurons that is not disclosed by any individual parent. In this case, the system exhibits synergistic dynamics, and the target neuron can be thought of as performing a kind of integrating “computation” on all of its inputs considered jointly (this is also sometimes referred to as “information modification” in the literature [19]). Conversely, if the whole is less than the sum of its parts, then there must be redundant information about Y instantiated multiple times over the parent neurons that is “double counted” when summing the marginals.
stops.paragraph: If the left-hand side of Equation (4) (the “whole”) is greater than the right-hand side (the sum of the “parts”), then there is some information about Y that is disclosed by the joint state of all the neurons that is not disclosed by any individual parent. In this case, the system exhibits synergistic dynamics, and the target neuron can be thought of as performing a kind of integrating “computation” on all of its inputs considered jointly (this is also sometimes referred to as “information modification” in the literature [19]). Conversely, if the whole is less than the sum of its parts, then there must be redundant information about Y instantiated multiple times over the parent neurons that is “double counted” when summing the marginals. The way that these pieces fit together is illustrated in Figure 1.
stops.cue: Watch how the sum of individual inputs' information compares to the information in their joint pattern, and what that gap implies.

stops.quote: This inequality has been recognized for decades; however, it was not until the seminal work of Williams and Beer [1] that it was recognized how to algebraically decompose the total joint mutual information into the particular contributions
stops.quoteFull: This inequality has been recognized for decades; however, it was not until the seminal work of Williams and Beer [1] that it was recognized how to algebraically decompose the total joint mutual information into the particular contributions of the parts (and higher-order ensembles of parts).
stops.paragraph: This inequality has been recognized for decades; however, it was not until the seminal work of Williams and Beer [1] that it was recognized how to algebraically decompose the total joint mutual information into the particular contributions of the parts (and higher-order ensembles of parts). Since its introduction, this framework, termed partial information decomposition, has been widely applied in fields from theoretical and computational neuroscience [9,21] to climate modeling [22] and sociology [23].
stops.cue: Note what breakthrough let researchers algebraically split total joint information into separate pieces.

stops.quote: Unfortunately, classical Shannon information theory provides no unique solution to any of these, and so considerable work has been devoted to developing formal measures of each.
stops.quoteFull: Unfortunately, classical Shannon information theory provides no unique solution to any of these, and so considerable work has been devoted to developing formal measures of each.
stops.paragraph: The result is an underdetermined system of linear equations, with three known values (the mutual information terms) and four unknown values (the partial information terms). If any of the unknown terms can be defined, then the other three emerge “for free”. Unfortunately, classical Shannon information theory provides no unique solution to any of these, and so considerable work has been devoted to developing formal measures of each. The most common approach is to define a redundancy function such as the original proposal of Imin [1] (for more on redundancy functions, see Section 4.3), although there have also been proposals that start with the unique information [24,25] or synergy [26,27].
stops.cue: Ask why ordinary information theory alone cannot pin down a single answer for redundancy.

stops.quote: In the absence of a single accepted measure, different contexts may require the choice of different functions.
stops.quoteFull: In the absence of a single accepted measure, different contexts may require the choice of different functions.
stops.paragraph: Applying PID analyses to real data requires some notion of redundant information (I∩(·)) to be operationalized. To date, no single universally accepted measure has been proposed. All measures have their own trade-offs and drawbacks (such as only being defined for systems of a fixed size, only being amenable to discrete random variables, or requiring arbitrary thresholds). There are, at present, close to a dozen competing redundancy functions (see [22,29,31–40]). In the absence of a single accepted measure, different contexts may require the choice of different functions. For example, having more than two predictors precludes the measures proposed in [24,31], while continuous data cannot be analyzed with the measures proposed in [24,40], and so on. The majority of the studies discussed in this paper used the original Imin measure proposed in [1], although this measure has been criticized for unintuitive behavior [29,39]. For a deeper discussion of the practical considerations, see Section 6.
stops.cue: Consider why no single redundancy measure might fit every situation.

stops.quote: The implication of this is that feedforward information propagation between source neurons and a target neuron is a reliable predictor of information processing.
stops.quoteFull: The implication of this is that feedforward information propagation between source neurons and a target neuron is a reliable predictor of information processing.
stops.paragraph: For example, one can ask whether synergy varies systematically as a function of the amount of information propagation—the transfer entropy from sources to a target—across triads. When we performed this analysis, examining 25 separate recordings at timescales varying from 1 ms to 14 ms, we found that synergy was strongly correlated (ρ ≫ 0.57 for all recordings and timescales; see Figure 4A). Interestingly, this analysis revealed that—for these recordings—the amount of synergy observed in a given triad was reliably about a quarter of the transfer entropy for that triad [2]. The implication of this is that feedforward information propagation between source neurons and a target neuron is a reliable predictor of information processing.
stops.cue: Look for what is being used as a stand-in for real information processing in these experiments.

stops.quote: Unambiguously, rich club triads processed more information than triads outside rich clubs. Numerically, the triads inside the rich clubs had 2.7 times the amount of synergy as the triads not in the rich club (Figure 4B).
stops.quoteFull: Unambiguously, rich club triads processed more information than triads outside rich clubs. Numerically, the triads inside the rich clubs had 2.7 times the amount of synergy as the triads not in the rich club (Figure 4B).
stops.paragraph: PID allowed us to test whether triads inside the rich club have greater synergy than those outside the rich club [2]. Unambiguously, rich club triads processed more information than triads outside rich clubs. Numerically, the triads inside the rich clubs had 2.7 times the amount of synergy as the triads not in the rich club (Figure 4B). Due to rich clubs having a high density of triads and rich club triads having a greater synergy per triad, a majority of the network-wide synergy was accounted for by rich club triads. Despite the fact that that less than 40% of the neurons were in the rich club, the rich club triads accounted for ∼88% of the network-wide synergy. We also found that there was a strong positive correlation between the rich club coefficient and the average synergy produced by rich club triads, suggesting that the rich club structure itself was related to the amount of computation.
stops.cue: Compare how much more joint computation happens inside densely connected hub triads versus outside them.

stops.quote: Using PID, we found that triads with more recurrent connections also had greater synergy [4]. Feedback connections were less predictive of synergy but tended to correlate with reduced synergy.
stops.quoteFull: Using PID, we found that triads with more recurrent connections also had greater synergy [4]. Feedback connections were less predictive of synergy but tended to correlate with reduced synergy.
stops.paragraph: Using PID, we found that triads with more recurrent connections also had greater synergy [4]. Feedback connections were less predictive of synergy but tended to correlate with reduced synergy. Numerically, in comparison to the simplest computational triads (those with no feedback or recurrent connections), triads with two recurrent connections and no feedback connections had 50% more synergy (Figure 4C). Triads with two feedback connections but no recurrent connections had 10% less synergy than the simplest computational triads. Modeling the synergy based on feedforward, feedback, and recurrent connection strengths instead of the numbers of connections, using multiple linear regression, revealed a similar pattern (Figure 4). The feedforward connections were found to be positively correlated with synergy and accounted for the most variance. The recurrent connections also were positively correlated, though they accounted for a smaller amount of the variance than the feedforward beta weights. This may be related to another prior finding that synergy is greater downstream of neurons that propagate information to many target neurons [28]. Finally, feedback connections were not significantly related to synergy. The finding that greater synergy is found in triads with greater connectivity between source neurons offers some perspective into why rich club triads are synergy-dense. Not only are rich club triads likely to have strong feedforward connections, they are also likely to have additional connections, including recurrent connections, that add to the overall synergy.
stops.cue: Notice how recurrent connections and feedback connections relate differently to synergy.

stops.quote: The result was unambiguous. The greater the mutual information between source neurons at the synaptic timescale, the greater the synergy [3]. More information processing occurs where similar information streams converge (Figure 4E, the thre
stops.quoteFull: The result was unambiguous. The greater the mutual information between source neurons at the synaptic timescale, the greater the synergy [3]. More information processing occurs where similar information streams converge (Figure 4E, the three leftmost panels for synaptic timescales).
stops.paragraph: In addition to questions about network topology, we also examined whether synergy varies based on the functional similarity of converging information streams. We tested whether there was a systematic correlation between the synergy of a triad and the mutual information in the source-neuron activities. Initially, we tested this for timescales in the synaptic range (<14 ms), consistent with the analyses described above. The result was unambiguous. The greater the mutual information between source neurons at the synaptic timescale, the greater the synergy [3]. More information processing occurs where similar information streams converge (Figure 4E, the three leftmost panels for synaptic timescales).
stops.cue: Track how synergy changes as the similarity between converging input streams increases.

stops.quote: Interestingly, synergy only increased up to a point. The peak in synergy occurred when the mutual information was about 7% of the maximal value, regardless of the timescale. Past this level, the synergy began to decrease (this level is mark
stops.quoteFull: Interestingly, synergy only increased up to a point. The peak in synergy occurred when the mutual information was about 7% of the maximal value, regardless of the timescale. Past this level, the synergy began to decrease (this level is marked by the vertical dotted line in Figure 4E).
stops.paragraph: To test whether synergy increases indefinitely as mutual information grows at longer timescales, we explored a range extending well past the synaptic range (time bins up to 2.25 s wide). Interestingly, synergy only increased up to a point. The peak in synergy occurred when the mutual information was about 7% of the maximal value, regardless of the timescale. Past this level, the synergy began to decrease (this level is marked by the vertical dotted line in Figure 4E). In the context of explaining the density of synergy in the rich club, the strong positive relationship between synergy and mutual information at synaptic timescales suggested that the activity of rich club neurons is generally more correlated than the activity of neurons outside the rich club. Indeed, rich clubs consist of a disproportionate number of inhibitory neurons with correlated spiking activity that synergistically predict the dynamics of the rest of the network [50].
stops.cue: Look for what happens to synergy once input similarity passes a certain level, and where that point falls.

stops.quote: This suggests that as the similarity of the converging information grows past some point, it becomes redundant, and the total amount of synergistic output is suppressed.
stops.quoteFull: This suggests that as the similarity of the converging information grows past some point, it becomes redundant, and the total amount of synergistic output is suppressed.
stops.paragraph: Leveraging the multiple outputs that PID offers, including redundancy as well as synergy, we were able to explore how the overall composition of information propagation varies across timescales [3]. As we lengthened the timescale, the total multivariate transfer entropy between the source neurons and the target neuron increased steadily across all timescales examined. As noted already, however, synergy increased only at the shorter timescales and decreased at the longer timescales. Observing the redundancy offered an explanation. Redundancy was positively related to mutual information at all timescales. Indeed, the slope relating the redundancy to mutual information became steeper at longer timescales (Figure 4E). This suggests that as the similarity of the converging information grows past some point, it becomes redundant, and the total amount of synergistic output is suppressed.
stops.cue: Consider why too much similarity between inputs might start suppressing synergy rather than helping it.

stops.quote: The researchers found that while brain activity was generally synergy-dominated (as opposed to redundancy-dominated), during movement execution (a reach-and-grasp action) the relative abundance of redundant information increased dramaticall
stops.quoteFull: The researchers found that while brain activity was generally synergy-dominated (as opposed to redundancy-dominated), during movement execution (a reach-and-grasp action) the relative abundance of redundant information increased dramatically.
stops.paragraph: The ability to assess how the structure of information processes changes in response to the demands of different tasks is a significant departure from the limitations of in vitro research. The researchers found that while brain activity was generally synergy-dominated (as opposed to redundancy-dominated), during movement execution (a reach-and-grasp action) the relative abundance of redundant information increased dramatically. This increase in relative redundancy was interpreted as a response to the practical requirements of the task: during motor execution, the brain needs to send the “move” signal to distant muscles, and to ensure high-fidelity transmission the brain may duplicate information many times over (minimizing the risk of a single corrupted signal leading to erroneous behavior). Similarly, different brain regions had different relative synergies during different tasks. For example, AIP (a pre-motor region) had the highest synergy during the fixation/cueing epoch, which then dropped off during movement, while M1 (the primary motor region) had the lowest synergy during the memory epoch, which then exploded during movement execution.
stops.cue: Notice what shifts in the balance of synergy versus redundancy during an actual movement.

stops.quote: These results show not only that synergistic information dynamics is a feature of ongoing, spontaneous neural activity but also that synergy seems to reflect behaviorally specific patterns of dynamical activity in the cortex.
stops.quoteFull: These results show not only that synergistic information dynamics is a feature of ongoing, spontaneous neural activity but also that synergy seems to reflect behaviorally specific patterns of dynamical activity in the cortex.
stops.paragraph: These results show not only that synergistic information dynamics is a feature of ongoing, spontaneous neural activity but also that synergy seems to reflect behaviorally specific patterns of dynamical activity in the cortex.
stops.cue: Ask what this pattern suggests about synergy's link to specific behaviors versus spontaneous activity.

stops.quote: One important caveat to note with respect to PID applied to neural data is that while it provides a powerful framework for recognizing statistical dependencies between neurons, it does not necessarily provide a mechanistic explanation for w
stops.quoteFull: One important caveat to note with respect to PID applied to neural data is that while it provides a powerful framework for recognizing statistical dependencies between neurons, it does not necessarily provide a mechanistic explanation for why particular neurons are synergy-dominated or redundancy-dominated.
stops.paragraph: One important caveat to note with respect to PID applied to neural data is that while it provides a powerful framework for recognizing statistical dependencies between neurons, it does not necessarily provide a mechanistic explanation for why particular neurons are synergy-dominated or redundancy-dominated. Now that the existence of statistical synergies is well replicated, a natural future avenue of research might be to attempt to determine how particular biological aspects of neuronal function (e.g., neurotransmitter systems, neural architecture, etc.) produce redundant, unique, or synergistic computational dynamics.
stops.cue: Look for what kind of explanation PID can and cannot give about why a neuron is synergy-dominated.

stops.quote: This sequence of numbers grows appallingly fast: in the case of six parent neurons, there are 7,828,354 distinct PI atoms, the vast majority of which are difficult to interpret.
stops.quoteFull: This sequence of numbers grows appallingly fast: in the case of six parent neurons, there are 7,828,354 distinct PI atoms, the vast majority of which are difficult to interpret.
stops.paragraph: The PID framework has a number of limitations that potentially complicate its application in naturalistic settings. The most significant is the explosive growth of the PI lattice. For a system with k parent neurons, the number of distinct PI atoms is given by the kth Dedekind number (minus two) [30]. This sequence of numbers grows appallingly fast: in the case of six parent neurons, there are 7,828,354 distinct PI atoms, the vast majority of which are difficult to interpret. Dedekind numbers greater than nine are currently unknown. Given that single neurons can receive inputs from very large numbers of upstream neurons, a “complete” description of the information dynamics of any individual neuron is completely intractable. This issue may be partially addressed by the development of heuristic measures of redundancy and synergy such as the O-information [65], which has been applied to information dynamics in networks of neurons [66] and human functional magnetic resonance imaging blood-oxygen-level-dependent (fMRI-BOLD) signals [67], although these measures typically trade completeness for scalability.
stops.cue: Note how quickly the number of distinct information components grows as more input neurons are added.

stops.quote: The existence of synergy in empirical data shows us that neurons do not appear to blindly sum the number of inputs and fire in response to the total (as would be expected from a basic threshold model or complex contagion model), but instead
stops.quoteFull: The existence of synergy in empirical data shows us that neurons do not appear to blindly sum the number of inputs and fire in response to the total (as would be expected from a basic threshold model or complex contagion model), but instead they are also sensitive to the particular patterns of incoming stimuli.
stops.paragraph: In this paper, we have aimed to provide an accessible introduction to the partial information decomposition framework [1] and shown how it can be applied to answer fundamental questions about information processing in neural circuits. We have focused particularly on statistical synergy, i.e., the information about the future of a target neuron that is disclosed by the higher-order patterns instantiated by multiple upstream neurons and is irreducible to any single source, as a measure of processing or computation. The existence of synergy in empirical data shows us that neurons do not appear to blindly sum the number of inputs and fire in response to the total (as would be expected from a basic threshold model or complex contagion model), but instead they are also sensitive to the particular patterns of incoming stimuli. Furthermore, not only does the existence of statistical synergy add nuance and dimensions to our understanding of the dynamics of individual neurons, we have also shown that the patterns of synergistic information processing are informed by the local environment in which those neurons are embedded (rich club membership, motifs, clustering, etc.), as well as the behavioral state of the oganism under study. These findings hint at the existence of a large, potentially fruitful space of future research relating higher-order information dynamics to biological, cognitive, systemic phenomena at many scales of analysis.
stops.cue: Consider what the presence of synergy implies about whether neurons simply add up their inputs.

stops.quote: Ball lightning appears seemingly random in time and space, lasts a few seconds, and disappears with traces or without. Because of its unpredictable occurrence, most of the collected material remains anecdotal.
stops.quoteFull: Ball lightning appears seemingly random in time and space, lasts a few seconds, and disappears with traces or without. Because of its unpredictable occurrence, most of the collected material remains anecdotal.
stops.paragraph: Since Sur le tonnerre of French astronomer and physicist François Arago (1837), the term ball lightning (Kugelblitz, foudre globulaire) stands for a still unexplained group of metastable luminous phenomena in atmospheric electricity. Ball lightning appears seemingly random in time and space, lasts a few seconds, and disappears with traces or without. Because of its unpredictable occurrence, most of the collected material remains anecdotal.
stops.cue: Notice what kind of traces ball lightning tends to leave, or not, when it vanishes.

stops.quote: Rakov and Uman (2003, p. 656, p. 658) characterized ball lightning as “a phenomenon for which there exists numerous witness reports but little, if any, scientific documentation such as photographs, videotapes, or other scientific recordings
stops.quoteFull: Rakov and Uman (2003, p. 656, p. 658) characterized ball lightning as “a phenomenon for which there exists numerous witness reports but little, if any, scientific documentation such as photographs, videotapes, or other scientific recordings.”
stops.paragraph: In chapter 20 of their lightning handbook, Rakov and Uman (2003) summed up the status quo on ball lightning. The authors were puzzled by 2400 references in Stenhoff’s book (1999), whereas their handbook on all lightning aspects comprises over 6000. This was also remarked by Thottapillil (2005, p. 31) in his COST Action proposal P18 on the physics of lightning together with 30 European researchers and the consensus that “the reality of ball lightning is not in doubt.” Rakov and Uman (2003, p. 656, p. 658) characterized ball lightning as “a phenomenon for which there exists numerous witness reports but little, if any, scientific documentation such as photographs, videotapes, or other scientific recordings.” They counted almost 5000 observation reports. “There may be more than one type of ball lightning and more than one mechanism by which ball lightning is generated”, they continue, also “There have been many theories devised to explain ball lightning. None is completely satisfactory” and “many luminous phenomena created in the laboratory are claimed by their creators to be ball lightning”. For the same reason, Turner called ball lightning research a “fragmented science” (2001).
stops.cue: Ask what kind of documentation is missing that would make this phenomenon more than anecdote.

stops.quote: Chances to monitor the transient phenomenon directly are minimal: Tompkins et al. (1975) searched about 12 000 photographic records of the US Prairie Meteorite Network that observed the night sky daily for over 10 years and found two probab
stops.quoteFull: Chances to monitor the transient phenomenon directly are minimal: Tompkins et al. (1975) searched about 12 000 photographic records of the US Prairie Meteorite Network that observed the night sky daily for over 10 years and found two probable ball lightning events.
stops.paragraph: Chances to monitor the transient phenomenon directly are minimal: Tompkins et al. (1975) searched about 12 000 photographic records of the US Prairie Meteorite Network that observed the night sky daily for over 10 years and found two probable ball lightning events. Other photographic or video records (e.g. 1935 Berlin; 1976 Transvaal, South Africa; 1978 Montafon, Austria; 1985 Lake Undugun, Russia; or 2003 Zwönitz, Germany) were also random products. Therefore, Singer (1971, chap. 5.B.2) and Stenhoff (1999, chap. 10.4) paid special attention to ball lightning reports coming from scientists or trained professionals. However, large databanks like Rayle’s (1966; N = 112 reports) and McNally’s (1966; N = 513 reports) from the US did not ask for observer’s professions and degrees. Published ball lightning reports of scientists are scattered, and even more remain unpublished.
stops.cue: Look at how rare a direct photographic catch of the event actually is, given the scale of the search.

stops.quote: Wilhelm von Haidinger, member of the Imperial Academy of Sciences at Vienna, observed ball lightning from his home at Vienna’s 3rd district Landstrasse on 20 October 1868, in a heavy thunderstorm between 17:15 and 17:30 LT
stops.quoteFull: Wilhelm von Haidinger, member of the Imperial Academy of Sciences at Vienna, observed ball lightning from his home at Vienna’s 3rd district Landstrasse on 20 October 1868, in a heavy thunderstorm between 17:15 and 17:30 LT
stops.paragraph: We start our series of cases with a chronology of eyewitness reports by natural scientists, and technical and medical experts. Several alleged observations (e.g. of Niels Bohr and Victor Weisskopf), often quoted in science or popular journals, were incorrect or lacked data: Tuck (1971) only wrote that he heard from Weisskopf that Bohr had once seen ball lightning. Martin Ryle was quoted without details by Davies (1987). Pyotr Leonidovich Kapitsa developed a ball lightning theory but reported no alleged sighting. Geologist and mineralogist Wilhelm von Haidinger, member of the Imperial Academy of Sciences at Vienna, observed ball lightning from his home at Vienna’s 3rd district Landstrasse on 20 October 1868, in a heavy thunderstorm between 17:15 and 17:30 LT: “The electric fireball was one of the very first discharges of the thunderstorm . . . It stood maybe 2–3 s in front of the right pane of the window . . . It is indeed simple to describe the ball, of a vivid yellow light, especially on the right . . . while on the left . . . clearly red, with longer rays than the ball, firing from it to the right and towards the earth, of red, yellow colour, up to the most dazzling white. Also, left there were shorter rays inclined obliquely towards the earth. . . . Several discharges followed and after [them] hail and rain.” Haidinger (see his sketch in Fig. 1) determined the object’s angular diameter as 0.83°. After his observation at Ungargasse 3, 3rd district, to the southwest, Haidinger heard about other occurrences in Vienna. Four of them sound like ordinary lightning but two described ball lightning: P. Joseph Dobner, Haidinger’s friend, took shelter from the thunderstorm in a friend’s home at Magdalenenstr. 32, 6th district. He saw a glaring blue sphere outside the window to the southeast. No more details are given. Another
stops.cue: Note the precision with which this observer records time and place for a fleeting event.

stops.quote: Gerlach also mentioned bluish “spraying” of electrical wires and blown fuses in “a whole row of houses” (Gerlach, 1927). His speed calculation of 1225 m s−1 is quite amazing, because it means the object travelled at a speed of Mach 3.6 “sou
stops.quoteFull: Gerlach also mentioned bluish “spraying” of electrical wires and blown fuses in “a whole row of houses” (Gerlach, 1927). His speed calculation of 1225 m s−1 is quite amazing, because it means the object travelled at a speed of Mach 3.6 “soundless”, without an acoustic effect (sonic boom). This is one of the rare occasions where ball lightning met a gifted experimental physicist.
stops.paragraph: Walther Gerlach, physics professor at the University of Tübingen, wrote a report to Naturwissenschaften on 20 May 1927: “On 9 May 1927, 08:00 [LT] I observed ball lightning [at Tübingen] . . . I happened to stand at the window . . . In the northeast, linear lightning went down with strong ramifications. From it (apparently out of a sharp kink) came a bright luminous yellowish-white ball in a considerable height and flew to the southwest. The time between lightning and the ball’s flyover of our institute was roughly 1 s. It could be observed for another second in the same appearance on its straight trajectory, soundless. Two seconds later, a not very strong thunder started, and 1.5 s after its start, there was an extraordinarily violent detonation, like an explosion bang.” Gerlach did his calculations: with a speed of sound of 330 m s−1 and observed times of the lightning’s thunder and the explosion, he got a ball lightning trajectory of 1300 + 1150 = 2450 m. In 2 s flight time, “ball lightning had a mean speed of about 1200 m s−1”. “I learnt at noon that the ball hit a small, barn-like house on the edge of Tübingen which is 1100 m distant . . . the top of an electrical mast was smashed nearby.” Gerlach also mentioned bluish “spraying” of electrical wires and blown fuses in “a whole row of houses” (Gerlach, 1927). His speed calculation of 1225 m s−1 is quite amazing, because it means the object travelled at a speed of Mach 3.6 “soundless”, without an acoustic effect (sonic boom). This is one of the rare occasions where ball lightning met a gifted experimental physicist. Gerlach is renowned for his 1922 experiment about spin quantization in a magnetic field.
